definition: The physical parts of a computer, such as chips, boards, disks, cables, and the power supply.
wrongs: Programs and data that tell the machine which tasks to perform.
A named collection of bytes stored under a single filename.
Rules that two computers follow when they exchange messages.
why: Hardware is the tangible equipment that stores, moves, and processes data.
example: Opening a lab desktop shows a processor package, memory modules, a disk, and a power supply.
scenario: A checklist names a mouse, a keyboard, and a monitor. Classify those three items.
scenarioWhy: A mouse, a keyboard, and a monitor are physical parts of the computer system.

definition: Programs and related data that instruct the hardware which tasks to perform.
wrongs: The metal chassis, chips, and cables inside the machine.
The wall outlet that supplies electrical power.
A cooling fan bolted to the processor heat sink.
why: Software is the instructions and data, while the chips and cables only carry out those instructions.
example: A photo editor installed on a laptop tells the machine how to crop and save pictures.
scenario: A student installs a spreadsheet package on a laptop. Classify that package.
scenarioWhy: An installed spreadsheet package is a program, so it is software.

definition: The processor that fetches instructions from memory and carries them out.
wrongs: The long-term disk that keeps files after power is removed.
The screen that displays pixels to the user.
The board that only supplies fan power.
why: The processor is the component that reads instructions and executes them.
example: A laptop chip marked with a model number performs the steps of a running calculator program.
scenario: A machine must fetch and perform each instruction of a loaded program. Which component does that work?
scenarioWhy: Fetching and performing instructions is the job of the processor.

definition: The processor section that performs arithmetic and logical operations on data.
wrongs: The section that only decides which instruction to fetch next.
The disk controller that schedules platter reads.
The pixel array that forms an image on a screen.
why: Addition, subtraction, and logical tests are carried out by the arithmetic and logic section of the processor.
example: During a payroll run, the processor adds hours times wage inside its arithmetic section.
scenario: A program adds two integers. Which processor section performs that addition?
scenarioWhy: Integer addition is an arithmetic operation, so the arithmetic and logic section performs it.

definition: The processor section that fetches instructions and directs the other parts to carry them out.
wrongs: The section that only adds and compares numeric values.
The fan controller on the power supply.
The pixel clock inside a monitor.
why: The control section generates the signals that sequence fetch, decode, and execute.
example: On each tick, signals from the sequencing section open the path that loads the next instruction.
scenario: Someone must direct fetch and decode, rather than add the numbers. Which processor section does that directing?
scenarioWhy: Sequencing fetch and decode is the role of the control section.

definition: The working store that holds instructions and data of programs while they are running.
wrongs: The printer tray that holds sheets of paper.
The keyboard buffer that only stores the last key.
The cooling duct that moves air across the case.
why: A running program is loaded into the working store so the processor can fetch its instructions.
example: After a browser launches, its code and open tabs occupy the computer's working store until it exits.
scenario: After a program is launched, the processor fetches its instructions from which store?
scenarioWhy: Instructions of a running program are fetched from the working store, not from an output device.

definition: Read-write working memory that can be accessed in any order and loses its contents when power is removed.
wrongs: Read-mostly memory that keeps startup code after power is removed.
Magnetic platters that keep files for years without power.
A paper listing of hex dumps stored in a binder.
why: Ordinary main memory can be read or written at any address and is volatile.
example: Unplugging a desktop clears the unsaved contents of its memory modules even though the disk files remain.
scenario: A technician removes power and the working memory modules forget their contents. Which memory behavior is that?
scenarioWrongs: Startup memory that keeps its code
scenarioWhy: Memory modules that can be rewritten and that forget their contents at power-off are ordinary working memory.

definition: Non-volatile memory that keeps fixed data, such as startup code, and is mainly read during operation.
wrongs: Working memory that is wiped every time power is removed.
A spinning platter used for user documents.
A temporary cache that holds only the newest pixels.
why: Startup code must remain when the machine is off, so it is kept in non-volatile read-mostly memory.
example: A motherboard still contains its startup program after the power cord has been unplugged overnight.
scenario: Startup code must survive a power loss and is not rewritten during normal class use. Where is that code kept?
scenarioWhy: Code that remains without power and is mainly read fits non-volatile startup memory.

definition: A small, fast memory that keeps copies of data the processor is likely to need again soon.
wrongs: A high-capacity disk used to archive course videos.
The paper manual shipped with a printer.
A network cable that carries packets between rooms.
why: Keeping recent data close to the processor avoids waiting for slower main memory.
example: A tight loop adds the same total repeatedly, and the processor finds that total in its small fast memory instead of DRAM.
scenario: A loop reuses one total many times, and the processor keeps a copy in a small fast store beside itself. Name that store's role.
scenarioAnswer: A fast copy of likely data
scenarioWhy: A small fast store of reused values is a cache sitting close to the processor.

definition: High-capacity non-volatile storage that keeps programs and files when they are not active in main memory.
wrongs: A handful of registers inside the processor.
The small fast copy store next to the processor.
The volatile modules that forget data at power-off.
why: Disks and flash drives retain large amounts of data after power is removed.
example: A student shuts down the lab PC, and the essay on the internal drive is still there the next morning.
scenario: An essay must remain after shutdown and is far larger than working memory. Which class of store should hold it?
scenarioWhy: A large file that must survive shutdown belongs in long-term high-capacity storage.

definition: A device that sends data from the outside world into the computer.
wrongs: A device that only presents results from the computer to people.
A program that edits photographs.
A cable standard used only inside the processor package.
why: Keyboards, mice, and scanners supply data to the computer rather than display results.
example: A barcode scanner at a checkout sends each product code into the point-of-sale computer.
scenario: A barcode scanner sends product codes into a checkout computer. Which role does the scanner play?
scenarioWhy: A scanner supplies external data to the computer, so it brings data in.

definition: A device that presents results from the computer to the outside world.
wrongs: A device that only sends keystrokes into the computer.
The working memory that holds a running program.
The startup chip that stores boot code.
why: Displays, printers, and speakers deliver processed results to people or other equipment.
example: A classroom projector shows the laptop's slides on the wall during a lecture.
scenario: A projector shows slides that come from a laptop. Which role does the projector play?
scenarioWhy: A projector delivers the computer's images to the room, so it presents results.

definition: A device attached to the computer to add input, output, or extra storage.
wrongs: The arithmetic section inside the processor.
The core of the operating system.
A number system that uses digits 0 and 1.
why: Printers, webcams, and external drives are attached devices, not the processor itself.
example: A USB webcam clipped to a monitor plugs into the PC and captures the lab bench.
scenario: A USB webcam sits outside the main case and plugs into the computer. How should it be classified?
scenarioWrongs: The core of the operating system
scenarioWhy: A webcam attached from outside the case is an extra device, not part of the processor.

definition: The shared address, data, and control lines that connect the processor, memory, and input/output.
wrongs: A program that translates source code before it runs.
A folder that groups related documents.
A character code for English letters.
why: The processor, memory, and devices exchange addresses, data, and control signals over shared lines.
example: A memory read places an address on one set of lines and the stored byte returns on another set.
scenario: The processor, memory, and devices must share pathways for addresses, data, and control signals. Name that pathway group.
scenarioWhy: Addresses, data, and control signals travel on the shared lines that connect the main parts.

definition: A stored-program design in which instructions and data share one memory and travel over a common bus.
wrongs: A design with separate memories and buses for instructions and for data.
A network in which every office is linked across several countries.
A screen layout built only from windows and icons.
why: The classic stored-program computer keeps instructions and data in the same memory.
example: One memory chip holds both a small program and the numbers that program adds, and both travel over the same bus.
scenario: A teaching computer stores instructions and numbers in the same memory and uses one bus to fetch either. Name that organisation.
scenarioWhy: Sharing one memory and one bus for instructions and data is the stored-program organisation.

definition: The repeating sequence in which the processor fetches, decodes, and executes an instruction.
wrongs: The power-on sequence that loads the operating system once.
The handshake two computers use to open a connection.
The steps a user follows to rename a folder.
why: Every instruction is handled by repeating fetch, decode, and execute.
example: A counter program repeatedly loads the next ADD, interprets it, and updates the total.
scenario: The processor repeats fetch, decode, and execute for every ADD in a loop. Name that repeating sequence.
scenarioWhy: Fetch, decode, and execute is the sequence applied to each instruction.

definition: System software that manages hardware and provides services so application programs can run.
wrongs: A single drawing program used to make a poster.
The physical board that holds the processor socket.
A numeric label such as 192.168.1.10.
why: Applications rely on the operating system to manage memory, files, and devices.
example: When two apps open at once, the installed system software decides which one gets the processor next.
scenario: Several applications run at once and something must manage memory, files, and devices for them. Which software does that?
scenarioAnswer: The system manager for hardware and apps
scenarioWhy: Managing memory, files, and devices for applications is the role of the operating system.

definition: A program that helps a user carry out a task, such as writing, calculating, or browsing.
wrongs: The privileged core that schedules processes and manages memory.
Startup code stored in a non-volatile chip on the board.
A device driver that only talks to a disk controller.
why: Word processors and browsers serve user tasks rather than operating the hardware directly.
example: A student writes a lab report in a word processor and checks spelling as they type.
scenario: A student writes a report in a word processor. Which class of program is that word processor?
scenarioWhy: A word processor helps the user write, so it is a user-task program.

definition: Software that operates and supports the computer, including the operating system and device drivers.
wrongs: A game the user plays after class.
A photo stored in a folder of pictures.
The metal case around the motherboard.
why: Drivers and the operating system support the machine itself rather than a single user hobby.
example: A disk driver loaded at startup lets the rest of the machine read and write the internal drive.
scenario: A driver lets the machine talk to a disk controller. Which class of software is that driver?
scenarioWhy: A disk driver supports the computer hardware, so it is support software.

definition: A named collection of data stored as one unit on a storage device.
wrongs: A container that groups several named collections and other containers.
A single binary digit that is either 0 or 1.
The shared lines linking the processor and memory.
why: The file system stores a document or photo as one named unit of bytes.
example: A student saves a photo on a USB stick under the name campus.png.
scenario: A photo is stored on a drive as one named sequence of bytes called campus.png. Name that stored unit.
scenarioWrongs: The lines between processor and memory
scenarioWhy: One named sequence of bytes stored on a drive is a file.

definition: A named container that groups files and other containers on a storage device.
wrongs: One photo stored by itself under a single filename.
An eight-bit group used as a typical memory location.
A base-16 digit written with symbols 0 through F.
why: Folders exist so related files can be grouped under one name.
example: The name Lab1 on a drive contains three report documents and nothing else is stored beside those names.
scenario: Three lab reports are grouped under the single name Lab1 on a drive. Name that grouping.
scenarioWhy: Lab1 groups several reports, so it is a container of files.

definition: A single binary digit that holds either 0 or 1.
wrongs: A group of eight binary digits.
A group of four binary digits.
A base-10 digit that may be from 0 through 9.
why: The smallest unit of stored data is one binary digit.
example: A door sensor records only closed as 0 and open as 1 in a status flag.
scenario: A door sensor stores only the digit 0 or the digit 1. Name that unit of data.
scenarioWhy: A lone 0 or 1 is one binary digit.

definition: A group of eight bits, the usual size of one addressable memory location.
wrongs: A single binary digit.
A group of four bits.
A group of sixteen bits.
why: Modern computers address memory in units of eight bits.
example: The letter A in a plain English text file occupies eight bits in memory.
scenario: One addressable memory location holds eight binary digits. How many bits is that location?
scenarioWhy: The usual addressable location is eight bits.

definition: A binary storage unit equal to 1024 bytes, the size commonly used when measuring memory.
wrongs: A unit equal to 1000 bits.
A unit equal to 8 bytes.
A unit equal to 1024 bits.
why: Memory sizes use powers of two, and 2 to the power 10 is 1024 bytes.
example: A tiny text buffer is described as 1 KB because it holds 1024 bytes under the binary convention.
scenario: Using the binary memory convention, how many bytes are in 1 KB?
scenarioWhy: In the binary convention used for memory, 1 KB is 2 to the power 10 bytes, which is 1024.

definition: A base-2 place-value system that uses only the digits 0 and 1.
wrongs: A base-10 system that uses digits 0 through 9.
A base-16 system that uses digits 0 through 9 and A through F.
A base-8 system that uses digits 0 through 7.
why: Digital circuits have two stable states, so values are written in base 2.
example: A row of four switches encodes the number thirteen as the pattern 1101.
scenario: A value is written using only the digits 0 and 1, and each place is worth twice the place on its right. Name that system.
scenarioWhy: Digits 0 and 1 with places that double are base 2.

definition: A base-16 place-value system whose digits run from 0 through 9 and A through F.
wrongs: A base-2 system whose only digits are 0 and 1.
A base-8 system whose digits run from 0 through 7.
A base-10 system whose digits run from 0 through 9.
why: Each hex digit replaces exactly four bits, which shortens long binary patterns.
example: A programmer writes the eight-bit pattern 11111111 as FF in a memory dump.
scenario: The byte pattern 11111111 is written as FF. Which base uses the digit F?
scenarioWhy: The digit F belongs to base 16, where it means fifteen.

definition: A base-8 place-value system that uses the digits 0 through 7.
wrongs: A base-2 system that uses only 0 and 1.
A base-10 system that uses 0 through 9.
A base-16 system that uses 0 through 9 and A through F.
why: Each octal digit replaces a group of three bits.
example: The permission triple 755 is written with digits that never exceed 7.
scenario: A permission code uses only digits 0 through 7, and each digit stands for three bits. Name that base.
scenarioWhy: Digits limited to 0 through 7 form base 8.

definition: A base-10 place-value system that uses the digits 0 through 9.
wrongs: A base-2 system that uses only 0 and 1.
A base-8 system that uses only 0 through 7.
A base-16 system that uses 0 through 9 and A through F.
why: Everyday counting uses ten digits, so each place is worth ten times the place on its right.
example: A price tag shows 249, and each digit is one of 0 through 9.
scenario: A price uses digits 0 through 9, and each place is worth ten times the place on its right. Name that base.
scenarioWhy: Digits 0 through 9 with places that scale by ten are base 10.

definition: A 7-bit character code that represents English letters, digits, and common symbols.
wrongs: A character standard that assigns codes to most of the world's writing systems.
A base-16 shorthand for binary patterns.
A picture format that stores rows of colored dots.
why: The original American code uses seven bits, enough for English letters and common symbols.
example: In a plain English file, the uppercase letter A is stored as the code value 65.
scenario: An old terminal stores English letters in 7 bits, and uppercase A has code 65. Name that character code.
scenarioWrongs: A code set for the world's writing systems
scenarioWhy: Seven-bit codes for English letters, with A equal to 65, identify the classic English character code.

definition: A character standard that assigns code points to symbols from most of the world's writing systems.
wrongs: A 7-bit code limited to English letters, digits, and common symbols.
A 5-bit teleprinter code used for early telegraphy.
A dot-and-dash signaling method used on a telegraph key.
why: One standard must cover many languages, so its code space is far larger than seven bits.
example: A single document contains Chinese characters, Arabic letters, and an emoji, all with assigned code points.
scenario: A document must encode Chinese, Arabic, and emoji in one character standard. Which standard is built for that?
scenarioWhy: Chinese, Arabic, and emoji need a character standard far larger than the English 7-bit code.

definition: A translator that converts an entire high-level program into machine code before the program runs.
wrongs: A tool that executes source code one statement at a time.
A tool that only combines already translated pieces into one executable.
A tool that loads an executable into memory and starts it.
why: Compilation produces a machine-code result from the whole source program before execution.
example: A student clicks Build, waits while every source file is translated, and then runs the finished executable.
scenario: A language tool translates an entire source program into machine code, and only then is the program run. Name that tool.
scenarioWrongs: A loader that starts an executable
scenarioWhy: Translating the whole program into machine code before running it is compilation.

definition: A program that reads and executes source code statement by statement.
wrongs: A translator that converts the entire source program before execution begins.
A chip that performs arithmetic inside the processor.
A drive that stores files on flash chips.
why: An interpreter does not require a separate full machine-code file before it can run the source.
example: A classroom language tool runs each typed line of a script immediately, without writing an executable file.
scenario: A language tool executes a script one statement at a time and never writes a separate machine-code file. Name that tool.
scenarioWrongs: The arithmetic section of the processor
scenarioWhy: Executing source one statement at a time, without a separate machine-code file, is interpretation.

definition: A finite, ordered set of unambiguous steps that solves a problem or computes a result.
wrongs: The physical chips that execute instructions.
A cable that links two computers in one room.
A picture element on a display.
why: An algorithm is the procedure itself, independent of any one programming language.
example: To find the oldest student, a tutor writes ordered steps that scan a list once and remember the maximum age.
scenario: A tutor writes a finite list of unambiguous steps that finds the oldest student in a roster. Name that list of steps.
scenarioWhy: A finite ordered set of steps that solves a problem is an algorithm.

definition: The main circuit board that connects the processor, memory, buses, and expansion slots.
wrongs: A magnetic drive with spinning platters.
A flash drive with no moving parts.
A display panel that shows pixels.
why: The processor socket, memory slots, and chipset are mounted on the main board.
example: Inside a desktop, one large green board holds the processor socket, two memory slots, and the expansion connectors.
scenario: Inside a desktop, one board holds the processor socket, memory slots, and expansion connectors. Name that board.
scenarioWhy: The board that ties the processor, memory, and slots together is the main system board.

definition: Software stored in non-volatile memory on a device, such as the startup code on a motherboard.
wrongs: A spreadsheet the user edits and then deletes.
Volatile working memory that is empty after power-off.
A paper manual kept on a shelf.
why: Firmware stays with the hardware in non-volatile memory and controls that hardware.
example: Updating the motherboard startup program rewrites a chip on the board, and the new code remains after power-off.
scenario: Startup code lives in a non-volatile chip on the board and controls the hardware. Which software category is that code?
scenarioWhy: Software kept in a device's non-volatile memory is firmware.

definition: A secondary-storage device that records data as magnetic regions on spinning platters.
wrongs: A storage device that keeps data in flash chips and has no spinning platter.
Volatile memory modules used as the working store.
A chip that only holds startup code.
why: The read head senses magnetic patterns on rotating platters.
example: A lab server clicks softly as its platters spin, and a magnetized coating holds the course archive.
scenario: A drive stores the course archive as magnetic regions on spinning platters. Which drive type is it?
scenarioWrongs: A flash-chip drive with no platter
scenarioWhy: Magnetic regions on spinning platters identify a hard disk drive.

definition: A secondary-storage device that stores data in flash memory and has no spinning platter.
wrongs: A drive that records data magnetically on rotating platters.
A disc read by a laser from a reflective surface.
Working memory that loses data when power is removed.
why: Flash chips retain files without mechanical motion.
example: A thin laptop stores the operating system in flash chips, and nothing inside that drive spins.
scenario: A laptop drive keeps the operating system in flash chips and contains no spinning platter. Which drive type is it?
scenarioWhy: Flash chips with no spinning platter identify a solid-state drive.

definition: A network that connects computers within a small area such as a room, lab, or single building.
wrongs: A network that links sites across cities or countries.
A single file shared by email attachment.
A character code for English text.
why: Local networks cover a limited physical area and are usually owned by one organization.
example: Twenty lab PCs in one building share a switch and exchange files without leaving the campus wing.
scenario: Twenty computers in one building share a switch and do not need a telecom link between cities. Which network scope is that?
scenarioAnswer: A network inside a small area
scenarioWhy: Computers connected within one building form a local-area network.

definition: A network that connects computers across a large geographic area, such as cities or countries.
wrongs: A network limited to one room or one building.
A folder stored on a single disk.
A processor clock rating in gigahertz.
why: Long-distance links, often provided by a carrier, join distant sites.
example: A company connects its Yangon office and its Singapore office through a telecom provider.
scenario: Offices in two countries exchange data over a telecom provider. Which network scope connects them?
scenarioAnswer: A network across a large region
scenarioWhy: Sites in different countries joined by a carrier form a wide-area network.

definition: A numerical label that identifies a host on an IP network so packets can be delivered to it.
wrongs: A hardware address burned into a network interface by its maker.
A name such as example.com resolved by the naming system.
A small integer that selects one service on a host, such as 443.
why: Routers forward packets using the numerical IP label of the destination host.
example: A lab PC is configured as 192.168.1.10 so other machines on that net can send it packets.
scenario: A packet is addressed to the host numbered 10.0.0.5. Which kind of label is 10.0.0.5?
scenarioAnswer: A numerical host label on an IP network
scenarioWhy: A dotted decimal host number such as 10.0.0.5 is an IP address.

definition: A set of rules that governs how computers format and exchange messages.
wrongs: A finite list of steps for sorting a roster by hand.
A named container of files on a disk.
A physical plug on the side of a laptop.
why: Communication succeeds only when both sides follow the same message rules.
example: A browser and a web server both follow HTTP so a page request and the page response are understood.
scenario: A browser and a server follow HTTP so requests and responses have an agreed format. Name that kind of rule set.
scenarioWrongs: Hand steps for sorting a roster
scenarioWhy: HTTP is an agreed set of rules for exchanging web messages.

definition: A network arrangement in which a client requests a service and a server provides it.
wrongs: An arrangement in which equal peers both supply and request the same service.
A single computer that does all work with no network.
A bus inside one computer that links the processor and memory.
why: The client initiates the request, and the server listens and responds.
example: A browser on a student laptop requests a page, and a university web server sends that page back.
scenario: A browser requests pages and a web server responds with those pages. Name that arrangement.
scenarioWrongs: Equal peers sharing the same role
scenarioWhy: One side requests a service and the other provides it, which is the client-server arrangement.

definition: An interface that lets a person operate the computer through windows, icons, menus, and a pointer.
wrongs: An interface that accepts only typed text commands.
A translator that produces machine code.
A magnetic drive with spinning platters.
why: Pointing and clicking graphical objects is an alternative to typing commands.
example: A user deletes a file by dragging its icon to a trash picture instead of typing a command.
scenario: A user deletes a file by dragging an icon to a trash picture. Which interface style is that?
scenarioWhy: Dragging icons with a pointer is a graphical interface.

definition: An interface that lets a person operate the computer by typing text commands.
wrongs: An interface built from windows, icons, and a pointer.
Startup code stored in a non-volatile chip.
A small fast memory next to the processor.
why: The user types a command and the system prints a text response.
example: At a prompt, an administrator types a text command to list the files in the current container.
scenario: An administrator types a text command at a prompt and reads a text reply. Which interface style is that?
scenarioWhy: Typing commands at a prompt is a command-line interface.

definition: Memory that loses its stored contents when electrical power is removed.
wrongs: Memory that keeps its contents after power is removed.
Magnetic storage that retains files for years without power.
A paper printout stored in a folder.
why: Typical working memory and cache need power to hold their bits.
example: A power cut erases the unsaved numbers sitting in the working memory of a desktop calculator program.
scenario: A power cut erases unsaved numbers that were held only in the working memory chips. Which memory property explains that loss?
scenarioWrongs: Magnetic storage that lasts for years
scenarioWhy: Data that disappears when power is removed was held in volatile memory.

definition: Memory that keeps its stored contents after electrical power is removed.
wrongs: Working memory that is empty after a power cut.
A processor register that forgets its value without a clock and power.
A cache line that is lost when the machine is unplugged.
why: Startup chips and flash keep data with no applied power.
example: A phone still holds its stored photos in flash after the battery is removed.
scenario: Photos remain in a phone's flash chips after the battery is removed. Which memory property is that?
scenarioWrongs: A cache line lost when unplugged
scenarioWhy: Data that remains with no battery is stored in non-volatile memory.

definition: The start-up sequence that initializes hardware and loads the operating system into memory.
wrongs: Translating a whole source program into machine code.
Rearranging file fragments so they lie in order on a disk.
Converting a binary pattern into hexadecimal digits.
why: After power-on, firmware finds a bootable device and loads the operating system.
example: Pressing the power button runs the board's startup program, which then loads the operating system from the internal drive.
scenario: After the power button is pressed, firmware initializes the machine and loads the operating system. Name that sequence.
scenarioWhy: Initializing hardware and loading the operating system is the start-up sequence.

definition: The privileged core of an operating system that manages processes, memory, and devices.
wrongs: A web browser used to read documentation.
A text editor used to write source code.
A media player used to watch a lecture.
why: The kernel runs in privileged mode and provides the core resource-management services.
example: When an application asks for more memory, the privileged core grants pages and updates the process table.
scenario: An application asks for memory, and a privileged core grants it and schedules the next process. Name that core.
scenarioWhy: Privileged management of memory and processes is done by the kernel.

definition: A group of four bits, equal to one hexadecimal digit.
wrongs: A group of eight bits.
A group of sixteen bits.
A group of two bits.
why: Four bits can represent the values 0 through 15, which is exactly one hex digit.
example: The low half of the byte 3C is the hex digit C, and that half is four bits wide.
scenario: One hexadecimal digit represents a group of bits. How many bits are in that group?
scenarioWhy: One hex digit encodes four bits.

definition: The transfer of data between the computer and external devices such as keyboards and displays.
wrongs: The translation of an entire source program before it runs.
The conversion of a decimal value into base 2.
The grouping of files into a named container.
why: Input brings external data in, and output sends results to external devices.
example: A program reads a name from the keyboard and writes a greeting on the display.
scenario: A program reads a name typed at the keyboard and writes a greeting on the display. Name that exchange with external devices.
scenarioWhy: Reading a keyboard and writing a display moves data between the computer and external devices.
